items.old: BITCOIN MINERS (under construction) Miners decide on the order of transactions and confirm them by using the Proof of Work consensus algorithm to "mine" for new blocks for the blockchain. In essence, mining secures the Bitcoin network. This process uses lots of energy (mostly sustainable energy and energy that would otherwise be wasted — flare gas, stranded hydro-electric, etc.) in the form of electricity. Miners run the SHA-256 hashing algorithm — a one-way function that takes any input and produces a fixed 64-character output. They repeatedly hash block data + a random number (nonce) through SHA-256, checking if the result starts with enough zeros. It's not 'solving complex math' — it's a brute-force guessing lottery done at incredible speed. Once a miner finds a valid hash, the other miners will quickly validate this, and when it is accepted, a new block will be added to the blockchain. The miner (or mining pool) who successfully added the new block, gets a reward of (currently) 6.25 Bitcoin plus all the transaction fees for that block. This process happens roughly every 10 minutes (which is also known as the heartbeat of Bitcoin).

The subsidy started at 50 bitcoin and is cut in half every 210,000 blocks (about four years). Since the fourth halving, block 840,000 on 20 April 2024, the subsidy has been 3.125 bitcoin. The next halving is at block 1,050,000. A new block is found about every 10 minutes (the heartbeat of Bitcoin). https://mempool.space/api/block/0000000000000000000320283a032748cef8227873ff4872689bf23f1cda83a5

items.old: MEMPOOL The “holding area” of unconfirmed transactions in a Bitcoin node’s memory, waiting to be picked up by a Bitcoin miner and inserted into a block. DIFFICULTY ADJUSTMENT The code also has a difficulty adjustment that syncs every 2,016 block (approximately 2 weeks). What this does is it keeps the average block time to 10 minutes. If over the span of two weeks more mining power is added to the network, then the mining time will likely be below 10 minutes so the difficulty adjustment will make the algorithm a bit harder so the average time will likely go back up closer to 10 minutes for the next 2 weeks. This recalibration maintains the 10 minute "heartbeat" of Bitcoin. The difficulty level as of August 2020 is more than 16 trillion. That is, the chance of a computer producing a hash below the target is 1 in 16 trillion. To put that in perspective, you are about 44,500 times more likely to win the Powerball jackpot with a single lottery ticket than you are to pick the correct hash on a single try. Fortunately, mining computer systems spit out many hash possibilities. Nonetheless, mining for bitcoin requires massive amounts of energy and sophisticated computing operations. The maximum difficulty level is 2^224, an unimaginably enormous number that would take an unimaginably enormous amount of computing power to achieve. More on the difficulty adjustment: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Difficulty MINING REWARD The mining reward gets halved every 210,000 blocks (or roughly 4 years). The reward started at 50 Bitcoin when Bitcoin went live in 2009. The halving process will end in the year 2140 when all 21,000,000 Bitcoin have successfully been mined. From then on, the mining reward will only be transaction fees which should be fine considering there will be millions and millions of transactions every block by the time hyperbicoinization comes to fruition!

items.old: PREDICTABLE The supply issuance of Bitcoin is known in advance; it is written in the code of the protocol. The supply issuance gets cut in half every 4 years. Currently, 6.25 bitcoin get minted about every 10 minutes. In 2024, 3.125 bitcoin will get minted about every 10 minutes. Additionally, the supply cap is known. There will only ever be 21 million bitcoin, and no one can print more Bitcoin. There are no secrets or gatekeepers involved in Bitcoin.

items.old: BLOCK SIZE Each block in the Bitcoin Blockchain has a size of 1 MB (megabyte). Each block typically contains 1000-2000 transactions. The transactions awaiting verification/confirmation from the miners and the node operators are held in what is called the mempool. Currently, the entire Blockchain, which includes every single transaction that has ever occurred on the Bitcoin network up to the present moment (which updates automatically on all ), is over 300 GB. Satoshi knew that a block size larger than 1 MB would be inefficient (storage wise) as the nodes running the network wouldn't be able to cost effectively store the Blockchain if the blocks were larger. There was great controversy on this topic which led to a Bitcoin hard fork in 2017 called Bitcoin Cash. More on this hard fork can be found in (Block Size Wars (2015 - 2017)).
items.new: BLOCK SIZE Since SegWit (BIP 141, activated in 2017) a Bitcoin block is limited by weight: block weight must be at most 4,000,000 weight units. Non-witness bytes count three times and witness bytes count once, so a block of legacy transactions is still about 1 MB, while a block that uses SegWit can be larger than 1 MB on disk. Before SegWit the limit was 1 MB. How many transactions fit depends on their size. A figure of 1,000–2,000 (or 3,000–4,000) transactions assumed a flat 1 MB block and is not a protocol rule. Transactions waiting to be confirmed sit in the mempool. Every full node stores the chain of transactions. An older undated note on this page said that history was over 300 GB. That number is not a current measurement. Disagreement about raising the old 1 MB limit led to the 2017 hard fork that created Bitcoin Cash. More on that episode is in Block Size Wars (2015–2017). https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0141.mediawiki

items.old: A Bitcoin transaction is typically 300 to 400 bytes. 1,000,000 bytes in a megabyte. 1mb+ blocksize leaves room for 3000-4000 txs
items.new: A Bitcoin transaction is often a few hundred bytes. Since SegWit (BIP 141) the block limit is 4,000,000 weight units, not a flat 1 MB. A block made only of legacy transactions is still about 1 MB, which is room for a few thousand typical transactions. A block that uses witness data can be larger than 1 MB, so "1 MB leaves room for 3,000–4,000 transactions" is only a rough pre-SegWit sketch, not the current limit.

Types of Stable Coins:
Collateralized (USDC, Tether, BUSD) - 1:1 peg with USD. 100% fully reserved (they're supposed to be, at least). 
Algorithmic (UST Luna) - 1:1 peg with USD in a funky way. Whenever new UST is made they burn Terra Luna. When people redeem/sell UST to get dollars, new Terra Luna is minted (ex). It works when you're in a bull market. As long as the market cap of Luna is bigger than the market cap of UST, it is properly backed/pegged. On how the Luna coin pumped then dumped and more:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1MgH01Ni6O0
items.new:
Types of stablecoins:

Fiat-collateralized (USDC, Tether) — designed for a 1:1 peg with the US dollar and described by their issuers as reserved. This page does not audit those reserves.

BUSD is historical. On 13 February 2023 Paxos said that, as directed by the New York Department of Financial Services, it would stop issuing new BUSD on 21 February 2023. Paxos said outstanding BUSD would stay redeemable through Paxos Trust Company at least through February 2024.
https://www.paxos.com/newsroom/paxos-will-halt-minting-new-busd-tokens

UST (TerraUSD) is historical. It was an algorithmic stablecoin tied to LUNA: new UST was issued by burning LUNA, and redeeming UST minted new LUNA. That peg depended on the market treating LUNA as sufficient backing. In May 2022 the peg broke and UST and LUNA collapsed.
https://www.coindesk.com/learn/the-fall-of-terra-a-timeline-of-the-meteoric-rise-and-crash-of-ust-and-luna

Background video from around that collapse:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1MgH01Ni6O0

items.new:
This quote is from a 2019 study, not a current measurement. Foley, Karlsen, and Putniņš, in the Review of Financial Studies (2019), wrote that approximately one-quarter of bitcoin users were involved in illegal activity and estimated about $76 billion of illegal activity per year involving bitcoin (46% of bitcoin transactions), close to the scale of the US and European markets for illegal drugs. Their abstract also says the illegal share of bitcoin activity declines with mainstream interest in bitcoin and with the emergence of more opaque cryptocurrencies. The figures describe the period the paper studied. This page does not have a verified current replacement number.

items.old: (under construction) ETHEREUM IS A POOR LONG TERM INVESTMENT ETHEREUM IS NOT DECENTRALIZED Despite what Ethereum maxis say, and despite all the flashy marketing behind defi ("decentralized" finance), Ethereum is not actually decentralized. Ethereum is DINO (decentralized in name only). Here is why. Ethereum had a 70% premine. This means that 70% of the market supply is controlled by a handful of its early adopters who were given the opportunity to purchase thousands of Ether for exchange of 1 bitcoin. Roughly 31,000 bitcoin were exchanged (unconfirmed number). This happened before the network and mining went online, hence, a premine. More on the premine: https://www.coindesk.com/sale-of-the-century-the-inside-story-of-ethereums-2014-premine Here is a thread of arguments over the premine, if you're interested: https://twitter.com/hasufl/status/1280140252737343488 30% of Ethereum nodes are essentially controlled by three CEOs. Amazon, Alibaba, and Google control more Ethereum nodes than any other group on the planet. Venture Capitalists flock to Ethereum because they love control. 99.9% of ERC-20 tokens built on the Ethereum network are scams, pump-and-dumps, rug pulls and Ponzi schemes. History of dead coins prove this. See the list that grows every day: https://99bitcoins.com/deadcoins/ Any token built on top of the Ethereum network is not decentralized, despite what you're told. How can something be decentralized when its base layer, Ethereum, isn't decentralized itself? This just isn't possible. This is another reason why Bitcoin is so valuable. Any layer built on top of Bitcoin will be decentralized because its base layer is decentralized. This is VERY important!

items.old: (under construction) SIDECHAIN Sidechains are in fact something of a hybrid between layer 1 and layer 2 solutions to scaling. A sidechain is another blockchain that is linked to a main chain such as Bitcoin’s. They are linked with a two-way peg (2WP) that is a protocol that allows for the open transfer of cryptocurrency from the main chain to a layer two chain that requires a degree of third-party trust. One example of a sidechain is the Liquid Network, attached to Bitcoin’s main chain. Like other layer 2 scaling solutions, it aims to tackle scalability problems by offloading some of the validation and transaction processing processes to another blockchain. This frees up the main chain to take on a greater number of transactions. RSK Launched in 2018, RSK is a Bitcoin sidechain which can support Ethereum smart contracts. The RSK sidechain is “merge mined” with Bitcoin, meaning miners who mine Bitcoin's blockchain also contribute hash rate to mine blocks on RSK. @RSKsmart (twitter) https://www.rsk.co/ RSK's YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/c/RskSmart/videos

items.old: NODES (under construction) The Bitcoin nodes are simply computers that contain the Bitcoin Core code and the complete Bitcoin Blockchain (the transactional ledger/records history of transactions). There are currently about 14,000 Bitcoin nodes worldwide which speaks to the real decentralization and security of the Bitcoin network. There is no single point of failure to shut down Bitcoin. Nuclear war could (God forbid) wipe out 3/4 of the planet, but as long as one Bitcoin node is still functional, Bitcoin will continue to run uninterrupted. You could even find the first computer that ever downloaded the Bitcoin code (if it still exists) and destroy it; that wont matter. Bitcoin can not be stopped or deleted. WHAT NODES DO Nodes validate and process transactions on the Bitcoin network. When a bitcoin transactions happens, every node gets a veto to decide if this transaction was valid. They need to come to a full consensus on this vote- if any node decides a transaction is invalid, then the transaction doesn't actually occur. The role of a node is to communicate with the other nodes in the network directly, verifying that their history of transactions is aligned with the next node. As they verify new transactions, they check to see that the bitcoin being transacted has not been double-spent and that no bitcoin is being created out of thin air. If a node does see malicious transaction attempts, it along with the other nodes in the network will reject the transactions. Users (nodes), not miners or developers, decide which blocks are valid and which software to run.

As they verify new transactions, they check to see that the bitcoin being transacted has not been double-spent and that no bitcoin is being created out of thin air. If a node does see malicious transaction attempts, it along with the other nodes in the network will reject the transactions. Users (nodes), not miners or developers, decide which blocks are valid and which software to run.

For tax purposes as well as anti-money laundering (AML) regulations and counter terrorism financing (CTF) laws, custodial/regulated exchanges are forced to obtain personal identification from its users such as name, birthday, cell number, social security number, and photo ID. For privacy reasons, it is recommended that advanced Bitcoiners start to stack non-KYC Bitcoin (also known as "secret sats"). There are multiple ways to do this. Mining Bitcoin is an easy (but not so easy) way to earn KYC-free Bitcoin. See more in Bitcoin ATMs can also be used to purchase Non-KYC Bitcoin, find one near you here: https://coinatmradar.com/ Some Bitcoin ATMs require SMS verification. In order to stay KYC-free, you'll need to use either a burner phone not connected to your ID or the website https://textverified.com/ Also, make sure that the email address associated with your account and money you send to TextVerified isn't tied to your identity. You can pay in Bitcoin. I sent Bitcoin to my account via a lightning wallet that isn't tied to my identity. As you can see, getting KYC-free Bitcoin is a pain in the ass. On top of this struggle, Bitcoin ATMs charge outrageously high fees...usually around 8.4%. Non-KYC Bitcoin should be kept separately in a different wallet than your KYC Bitcoin; don't mix the stacks. Your non-KYC wallet should not be linked to your identity in any way else it ruins the purpose of a non-KYC stack. Over 40% since 2020 It's getting worse and worse Fiat currency in the United States started about 100 years ago. Quick history of the dollar: https://stacker.news/items/3009 The dollar as defined by the Constitution is a "weight of gold or silver." In 1913, the government inserted a permanent central bank called Federal Reserve to stand in between the Constitution and the people. This was the introduction of "the Fed dollar" or fiat currency. It is not a Constitutional dollar; it is a note that is issued by the Federal Reserve. This also gave the right to the Federal Reserve to print money whenever they wanted to. One dollar today was worth $0.04 in 1913, a reduction of purchasing power by 96% In the years past The Great Depression, through WWII, and after, the United States traded cash for gold from citizen and other nations. Eventually, those nations started asking for their gold back. In 1971 President Nixon decided to cut off other nations from their gold and we got off the Gold Standard. This is known as "The Nixon Shock." Our money wasn't backed by gold anymore. Instead, it was backed solely by the full faith and credit of the United States government. You had to trust the government. And while it helped America grow as a superpower … and helped many of us live lives of exorbitant privilege …It’s also responsible for the mess we’re in today. And it’s what will ultimately topple the US dollar. They say those who don’t know history are doomed to repeat it. But politicians know their history.

items.old: (under construction) SATOSHI NAKAMOTO Satoshi Nakamoto is the pseudonymous creator(s) of Bitcoin. His/their final public correspondence was a post on the bitcointalk.org forum on 12/12/2010: https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=2228.msg29479#msg29479 Satoshi’s final known private correspondence was from an April 26, 2011 email to Gavin Andresen. He wrote: "I wish you wouldn't keep talking about me as a mysterious shadowy figure, the press just turns that into a pirate currency angle. Maybe instead make it about the open source project and give more credit to your dev contributors; it helps motivate them." Theories as to why Satoshi disappeared: https://news.bitcoin.com/satoshis-final-messages-leave-tantalizing-clues-to-his-disappearance/ What we do know is that if Satoshi did reveal himself, he would have to sign the Genesis Block and create a verifiable PGP message to prove his/her identity.

items.new: PROOF OF WORK Bitcoin reaches agreement with proof of work, described in section 4 of the Bitcoin whitepaper. Miners spend energy to produce a hash below a target set by the network. Nodes follow the chain with the most accumulated work. Bitcoin still uses proof of work. Proof of stake is a different design, used by other systems, that picks block producers from holders of the asset instead of from work that was spent. https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf

items.new: PUBLIC KEY VS PRIVATE KEY A private key is the secret that can spend the bitcoin it controls. A public key is derived from that private key and can be shared. An address is derived from the public key. Knowing the address or the public key does not reveal the private key. If the private key, or the seed that generates it, is lost, that bitcoin cannot be spent. MULTI SIGNATURE WALLET A multi signature (multisig) setup is one that avoids a single point of failure in a normal hardware wallet. For example, in a 2/3 multisig setup, if one wallet gets compromised or lost, your bitcoin can still be accessed by use of the other two wallets combined.
